cut.what_it_is: A cut is a break in the skin that can bleed. Most small cuts can be treated at home.
immediate_steps: Wash your hands with soap and water, or use clean gloves, before touching the wound.
Apply gentle direct pressure with clean gauze or a clean cloth until the bleeding stops.
Raise the injured area above heart level if possible, to slow bleeding.
Once bleeding stops, rinse the wound with clean running water to remove dirt.
Cover with a clean bandage or dressing and change it daily or when wet or dirty.
avoid: Do not put toothpaste, turmeric, oils, powders or other household substances into the wound.
Do not use hydrogen peroxide or iodine to clean a fresh open wound.
Do not keep removing a dressing that has stuck to the wound.
Do not remove a large object stuck in the wound; press around it and get help.
good_signs: Bleeding stops within a few minutes of steady pressure.
Mild tenderness that improves day by day.
Edges of the wound slowly close and a dry scab forms.
warning_signs: Bleeding that soaks through the cloth or does not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure.
A deep or gaping wound, or an object stuck in it.
Numbness, weakness, or being unable to move the area.
Spreading redness, swelling, warmth, pus, red streaks, or fever (possible infection).
Dirty or rusty cause, or an animal or human bite.

burn.what_it_is: A burn is skin damage from heat, hot liquid, fire, chemicals or electricity. Minor burns affect only the top layer of skin.
immediate_steps: Move away from the source of the burn.
Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for about 10 to 20 minutes as soon as possible.
Remove rings, watches or tight items near the burn before swelling starts, unless stuck to the skin.
After cooling, cover loosely with a clean non-stick dressing or cling film.
Keep the area clean and watch it over the next days.
avoid: Do not apply ice or ice-cold water directly to a burn.
Do not apply butter, ghee, toothpaste, turmeric, oils or other household substances to a fresh burn.
Do not break blisters.
Do not peel off clothing that is stuck to the burn.
good_signs: Skin is red and sore but not blistered widely.
The area slowly heals without increasing pain or discharge.
warning_signs: A burn larger than the palm of the hand, or deep burns that look white, brown or charred.
Burns on the face, hands, feet, major joints or genitals.
Electrical or chemical burns, or burns from fire with smoke inhalation.
Signs of infection: increasing pain, pus, spreading redness or fever.
Burns in babies, young children or older adults.

bruise.what_it_is: A bruise is bleeding under the skin, usually caused by an impact. It changes colour as it heals.
immediate_steps: Rest the area and avoid activities that cause pain.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for short periods (about 10 to 20 minutes) in the first day or so to reduce swelling.
Raise the bruised limb if possible.
Protect the area from further knocks.
avoid: Do not put ice directly against the skin.
Do not massage a fresh or painful bruise hard.
Do not ignore severe pain after a hard fall or blow.
good_signs: Pain and swelling slowly reduce over several days.
The colour changes from red or purple to green and yellow as it heals.
Most bruises fade within about two weeks.
warning_signs: Severe pain, rapid swelling, or a very large bruise.
Numbness, loss of movement, or a limb that cannot bear weight (possible fracture).
A bruise that keeps getting bigger or does not improve in two weeks.
Any head injury with headache, vomiting, confusion or drowsiness.

safe_uses: Rinsing a cut after bleeding stops
Cooling a minor burn with cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes
avoid: Do not use dirty or contaminated water on an open wound.

safe_uses: Gentle direct pressure to stop bleeding
Wrapping a cold pack so ice never touches the skin
avoid: Do not use a visibly dirty cloth on an open wound.
Do not use gauze that is dirty or has been opened for a long time.
Do not wrap so tightly that fingers or toes turn pale, blue or numb.

safe_uses: Cold therapy for a bruise, wrapped in a cloth, for 10 to 20 minutes
avoid: Do not place ice directly on skin.
Do not use ice on a burn.

safe_uses: Washing your own hands before first aid
Gently washing the skin around a wound
avoid: Do not scrub soap deep into an open wound.

safe_uses: A thin layer on a cleaned minor cut before covering, if you are not allergic
avoid: Do not use on deep wounds or serious burns.
Stop if a rash or itching appears.

safe_uses: A thin layer on a cooled minor burn or a clean minor cut to keep it moist
avoid: Do not apply to a fresh burn before it has been cooled.

safe_uses: Soothing a cooled, minor burn with pure aloe vera gel
avoid: Do not use on open or broken skin.
Stop if irritation appears.

safe_uses: Loosely covering a cooled burn (lay it on, do not wrap tightly)
avoid: Do not wrap it around a limb tightly.

safe_uses: Gentle support for a bruised or swollen limb
avoid: Do not wrap tightly; loosen it if there is tingling, numbness or colour change.
Do not apply toothpaste to burns or cuts. It can irritate the skin and raise infection risk.
Do not apply butter, ghee or oils to a fresh burn or open wound. They trap heat and can cause infection.
Do not pack turmeric or other powders into a wound. They are not sterile and can cause infection.
